references.text: The first servant came and reported on his mina which had yielded ten minas in return ([ref:Luk 19:16-17|Luke 19:16-17]). The third servant stands in sharp contrast to him by having done nothing with his mina.

In Jesus' parable of the talents in [ref:Matt 25:24-25|Matthew 25:24-25], the lazy servant hides his talent in the ground, a parallel to the servant who hid the mina in a cloth. Both failed to manage what had been entrusted to them.
The servant justifies his passivity in [ref:Luk 19:21|Luke 19:21] with fear of his master, showing that hiding the mina in a cloth was motivated by fear rather than faithfulness.
The Lord's judgment on the servant in [ref:Luk 19:22-23|Luke 19:22-23] shows that leaving the mina unused in a cloth was completely unacceptable – he should at least have put the money in the bank.
The lazy person in [ref:Ordsp 26:13-16|Proverbs 26:13-16] finds excuses for his laziness, just as the servant in the parable justified his failure with explanations.
[ref:Jak 4:17|James 4:17] says that whoever knows what good they ought to do and does not do it, for them it is sin. The servant knew what was expected but failed to act.

In [ref:Matt 25:18|Matthew 25:18], the lazy servant buried his master's money in the ground, a direct parallel to the servant who hid the mina in a cloth – both expressions of neglecting entrusted responsibility.

The word "sweat-cloth" (σουδάριον) also appears in [ref:Joh 11:44|John 11:44], where Lazarus' face was bound with a sweat-cloth. It is the same Greek word used for the cloth in which the servant hid the mina.
The word σουδάριον is also used in [ref:Joh 20:7|John 20:7] about the face cloth that had been over Jesus' head in the tomb, the same Greek word as in Luke 19:20.
